utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will have objections with regard to this witness when you're prepared to hear them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the witness to whom you're referring, I assume, is John Sweeney. Can I take it, Ms. Moeller, that that is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before Mr. Sweeney is brought in, let me hear what Mr. Ackerman has to say in objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Sepenuk has a preliminary matter and then I have some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, I also had an objection, Your Honour, to certain portions of the statement, but I believe we've resolved it. I had objected to the first four paragraphs on page 10 of the statement. I spoke to Ms. Moeller about this before the session, and she has agreed to delete those four paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. So we can take our pens through these four paragraphs. Thank you. Now, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first objection I have regards page 9 of the statement, starting with the paragraph: "Their statements cross-corroborated ..." and every remaining paragraph of that page basically involves the opinions of this witness. I think it's inappropriate to have a witness come talk about the truthfulness of what people have told him. He talks about -- that it's his opinion that there had to be a plan for what he saw happen, happen, just a number of opinions. He's not brought here as an expert witness, he's not qualified as an expert witness, and has no business giving these kinds of opinions to this Court. I would therefore ask that those paragraphs all be excluded from his statement because they are opinion testimony, pretty much all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we're on -- this is all on page 9, is it, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it's page 9, from "Their statements cross-corroborated..." to the bottom, and then the first four of the next page have already been eliminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there are factual statements included in these paragraphs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, Your Honour. I found it very difficult to try to separate them out from the opinion, however, and I thought perhaps we could eliminate the whole thing; and if they're important enough to be dealt with, they can be dealt with live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's one way of doing it, Mr. Ackerman. Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I disagree with my learned colleague, respectfully. As Your Honour's already noted, there are several points of factual statements in there, and I don't see a need to take out the few parts that may not be factual, because I think this is not a jury trial, it's a trial, led by professional judges who are fully in a position to distinguish, having the full statement, between these elements that are fact elements and that can be given some evidentiary weight and others that may just be ignored when you finally come to your opinion about this trial. Maybe, if I may add in particular, in some paragraphs, in this part of the statement that Mr. Ackerman wants to delete, are two aspects in there that I actually intend to address with the witness, factual aspects of mass destruction which he saw himself and the displacement of Kosovo Albanian refugee which will be part of his testimony today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the parts that he's referred to, there is reference to the witness "being left in no doubt as to the truthfulness of the statements that had made to me." You would submit that's an appropriate piece of evidence for him to give?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I think it is his impression of the accounts he received from the persons he spoke to in Mala Krusa very -- and actually already in Albania, very close to the events. And I think it is fair for the witness to make up his mind about whether he would believe these people or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, speaking for myself, one paragraph that would concern me would be the third-last paragraph on the page. First of all, it would appear to be a form of expert evidence from someone who's not an expert; secondly, there's no factual basis set out for it and it would probably require weeks of evidence to set the factual basis for that particular conclusion, whereas the witnesses would undoubtedly be able to state the facts as he experienced them in relation to the events that this statement is mainly dealing with, and there are then conclusions that you can, no doubt, invite the Trial Chamber to draw about whether or not there was an organisation or a plan behind this. So we shall consider the position briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The only paragraph that we are prepared to exclude from admission at this stage is the one beginning, "At this time I have known Yugoslavia for eight years ..." We take the view that the very first paragraph to which Mr. Ackerman drew attention is problematic, but the issue of the weight to be given to any individual witness's assessment of the reliability of evidence given to him which he then relays to the Court is a matter that can only be addressed at the end of the day in this case when we come to assess all the evidence. And it's a matter on which submissions will undoubtedly be made by the parties at the end of the day, including submissions about the propriety of taking account of this sort of view. But it's not a view that we are prepared to exclude from admission at this stage; it's one to be taken into account, if appropriate, at the end of the day. So far as the rest of this page is concerned, the rest that attention has been drawn to, we consider that it would be wise of the Prosecutor to spend some time in live evidence with the witness so that, if there are any more particular objections that you wish to take, they can be taken at that stage. And if the Prosecutor fails to do so, then we are alert to the possibility of further submissions once you have cross-examined the witness. So we don't say for a moment, Mr. Ackerman, that there isn't some force in the point you make so far as what weight might be given to these sort of comments, and, indeed, do recognise you may make even stronger comments than simply to attack the weight that might be given to them. But we think that over the piece, these are issues for determination at the end of the case. We shall now hear from --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's not the end of my objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I said I had several, and I do. Your Honour, I appreciate what Ms. Moeller said about you all being professional Judges and I totally accept that; but the other side of that is we are in a court of law and there must be standards regarding the admission of evidence. I totally -- you know, I'm totally comfortable with you all reading what I'm trying to exclude here because I know, if you will exclude it, you will exclude it from your minds completely. But it should be excluded if you're going to do that. I want to go now to a bunch of video-clips that the Prosecution seeks to play to you today. These are all clips from -- I think from documentaries that were created by John Sweeney, who is, among other things, a documentary film-maker, with a certain view that he wanted to propagate to the world that doesn't necessarily, in all cases, fit with reality. The thing that I find inadmissible or maybe bizarre about the proposal to play these video-clips - and I assume Your Honours have the transcript of these clips there with you - it seems to me it makes no sense for the Prosecution to play, while John Sweeney is sitting on the witness-stand, John Sweeney making pronouncements on video. If they are things that he should be saying, then he should be saying them live here rather than on video. And many of the things he says on video are things that you'd never permit him to say here as a live witness; for instance, "Little Krusa is empty, abandoned, yet full of ghosts," and things like that. That goes all the way through this video. And mostly what they're going to play is John Sweeney talking. Occasionally somebody he's interviewing gets to say something, and in all cases these are people who have not been here and who won't be here and are people we'll never have an opportunity to cross-examine. I understand Your Honours can make your own evaluations regarding that, but it just seems to me that this is inappropriate. If John Sweeney is brought here to tell us what he saw when he visited Mala Krusa, then let him tell us what he saw when he visited Mala Krusa and not give us his opinions of what all he saw means. It just makes no sense to me that we would have to sit here and watch him pronounce on television what he might be able to say, if properly asked, during his live testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, this objection, I take it, relates to the material referred to also on page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think they have selected certain clips that they call clip 1, clip 2, clip 3, clip 10, clip 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9, ten clips from his video material. I don't think they intend to offer any additional video material; if they do, I have the same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: First of all, to clarify, we do seek to tender the full video documentaries, not only the clips; however, it's correct we selected a number of clips which are visual evidence. It is true that Mr. Sweeney speaks over the visual effect, but it is more the visual impact that Mr. Sweeney cannot describe as well as it is shown on the tape. For instance, when he walks through Mala Krusa, you see the state the houses were in, and this was the very week when UNMIK first entered Kosovo after the war. This was about a month before any exhumation team from this Tribunal ever came to this village. So it is very contemporaneous evidence, it is the best evidence that you could have, and I don't see that an oral description by Mr. Sweeney would replace such kind of evidence fully. The same relates to further clips we selected. The site where the hay-barn was standing, again, Mr. Sweeney was there a month before the exhumation team ever got there. He looked, in proofing, at the photos of the exhumation team and noted immediately that this was much later than when he was there, and the video does prove that it looked differently. The next video-clip we selected because Mr. Sweeney provides for the provenance of some documents that we wish to tender through him, which are mentioned in his statement; as well, the lists of Serbian names. And you can actually see in the video-clip how he physically seizes the material, and he explains what the material is. So there is a connection to tender this evidence. Then the next clip relates to pictures of the perpetrators he found, identifying the perpetrators who are appearing in these lists and duty rotas. The sixth video is a short scene showing forensic work in Mala Krusa, again contemporaneous evidence depicting some attempts made to exhume whatever was there still left to be found, and we have the exhumation report relating to this examination that we will seek to tender. Then we have two clips relating to the Drini River. One of the clips, again, Mr. Sweeney discovered a lorry which was half dumped into the Drini River and he got to this lorry, very closely, and made some discoveries that nobody else did. The exhumation team did not see or examine this lorry, but Mr. Sweeney saw it at this very early time. And the very last clip I selected is showing the victims who were killed in this incident, because we do not have any antemortem photos of these victims. And I would wish to tender this under the aspects of victim impact and also the aspects that some of these victims who have disappeared forever would be given a face. And that's what these clips are about. And I think it would be admissible to play them for the purposes that I have just outlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I respond very briefly, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree with Ms. Moeller that, if there are videos which will give you a better understanding of what Mala Krusa looked like when he went there, those are probably admissible, and I'd have no objection to those being shown in court without sound and he can describe them live. But we don't need the drama of his video presentation, his drama documentary, where he was taking a particular tack regarding this matter. I think that's for the Court to make the decision about. But he can describe what he saw, and I have no problem with that being shown in court that way. But his on-camera descriptions are a little strange, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, it's very difficult to simply exclude all the commentary because there will, no doubt, be parts of which are helpful in setting the factual position clear. When we heard a little part, I think, of the first of these videos yesterday, I think I detected on it rather somber and dramatic music that overlays some of the videos and films you see about Yugoslavia. I can assure you that, if anything, that simply alerts me to be very cautious about just how tendentious the presentation may, in fact, be rather than activating a button that becomes oversympathetic. So I think you need not worry about the Bench reacting inappropriately to comments that happen to be there, if, over the piece, the film is setting out the facts at a particularly relevant time and some of the commentary is of assistance in clarifying the facts. The one other matter that you may help us with, though, Ms. Moeller, is this: I am not, for one, prepared to spend time on 80 files of Mr. Sweeney's newspaper and broadcast comments without being directed to the particular relevance of the parts that you wish me to concentrate on. So you will not have from me a sympathetic ear to the reception of the two floppy disks that are referred to in the statement or the 40 VHS tapes. I'm assuming that you have selected for presentation to us in the clips the bits that you wish the Trial Chamber to consider and that the rest is simply the source material to which, if matters arise later, you would direct our attention to specific parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honours. I never intended to tender the two floppy disks or the 40 tapes of raw material. From this raw material I have selected one very short clip which relates to the lorry in the river, which is not in the documentation but which I think is very important first-hand evidence, and this is in this presentation. It has been given an exhibit number. But for the rest, none of this material is tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And that takes us, then, back to the two video broadcasts. Can we not take it that you've selected from them what is relevant and that it's not for us, then, on our own to explore these but simply to confine our attention to the parts that you play in court?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would respectfully seek to tender the full two documentaries because it contains a lot more useful and reliable, we submit, explanatory evidence. For instance, it also contains clips where two of the witnesses who have testified here as court witnesses, Mr. Ramadani and Mr. Krasniqi, appear in this tape and demonstrate on this tape how the incident happened. This may be useful corroborative evidence to their statements. And there is other material showing the village, the surroundings, and other things that we would submit is helpful to paint a full picture of the location and the events. We will not ask, Your Honours, however, of course, to rely on any conclusions drawn by Mr. Sweeney in this documentary or on any opinions he puts forward. And I think that may alleviate some of the concerns of my learned colleague Mr. Ackerman or the Court, hopefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will admit the video-clips. We will reserve our position on whether to admit the two videos in their entirety until the end of the examination-in-chief. We'll now hear from -- sorry, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I thought we might finish this witness a bit quicker if I take care of all matters before we have the statement submitted. Your Honour, I would seek the Court's guidance as to a part of the transcript that I have an objection to. It's on page 6 and deals with a very lengthy recitation of what Mr. Sweeney purports that an individual

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: page 7. Unlike the other persons that Mr. Sweeney talks about, this individual is not one who is coming before this Trial Chamber as an OTP witness and therefore is not available for cross-examination. The recitation of what Mr. Sweeney purports this witness stated or this person stated is not sworn, not under oath, but is being presented -- and I believe is the only source for these allegations. I think that that would go towards a violation of Rule 92 bis insofar as it's being submitted in written form, and it clearly is styled as if it were a

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: word and there doesn't appear to be anything in that section that Mr. Sweeney himself observed or heard from other people or confirmed through any independent or objective analysis. And insofar as it goes towards someone who, it might be argued, would be a subordinate of the accused, therefore I think it does constitute a violation of Rule 92 bis and what may be introduced in that regard. Again, this is the section that starts with: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The remaining paragraphs on page 7 -- the next paragraph on page 7, I think, can come in because we did have another witness who talked about that paragraph. But I think that the -- I see now that they've redacted a large portion of that in the newest version of the statement that we just received this morning. But I think that the remaining portions also ought to be taken out insofar as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you may have advantage over me. Are you saying that there is another version of this produced today?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have just been made aware that the redacted version that has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what's been redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Obviously the name of a certain witness was redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then there is also -- it looks like the last entire two paragraphs of page 6 have been redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we should probably go into private session as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me hear from Ms. Moeller first of all, Mr. Ivetic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We redacted that part of the statement for security reasons of another witness, and if I need to explain it further, we would need, indeed, to go into private session for a second. We did not redact it in order to take it out. We are not suggesting that this should not be part of the statement. And if you will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. So as far as we are concerned, the statement remains as it was, and the redaction is simply to ensure that there is no prejudice to security.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. On your remark yesterday that we should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- attempt to have a speedy, unredacted version ready of statements we tender under seal, we had this prepared for this witness today already, and this is what Mr. Ivetic just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Ivetic, going on to page 7, what are you saying about the top two paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, they are a continuation of the statement of the individual. I think we are going to need to redact something that Your Honour and I mentioned previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. What, this morning or --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This afternoon, Your Honour. I just realised something and that's why I wanted to go into private session to direct as to what needs to be redacted from our discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's go to private session for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Ivetic, I thought you were saying that the first two paragraphs on page 7 fell into a different category. Are you saying that they also --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They're just a continuation of the same portion and so I think that they fall under the same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, Ms. Moeller, what's your response to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: My response to that would be that this is first-hand hearsay evidence and, under the Rules of this Tribunal, admissible, and that this is no reason to exclude this kind of evidence. We have a range of jurisprudence on hearsay evidence in the Tribunal and -- for instance, the Appeals Chamber in the Aleksovski decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I put a particular question. What you say may apply to the first paragraph that we're looking at. But what's the position when the evidence that's hearsay contradicts the evidence of an eye-witness who has given evidence here in court? Should that be admissible?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: As far as I'm familiar with the jurisprudence, it does not exclude the admissibility but it goes to the weight of the evidence. And there is jurisprudence saying that usually live evidence will have a greater weight than hearsay evidence, and I think that's also a rule that applies, more or less, universally in legal systems. But according to the jurisprudence here, I don't think it would be a reason to exclude the evidence from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in admitting the statement, we will admit these various paragraphs, but we draw attention to the jurisprudence of the Tribunal which essentially would normally prefer the evidence of a witness who has come here to be cross-examined to that of a witness whose evidence is expressed by another hearsay where cross-examination of the true source of the evidence is not possible. So we are particularly alert to the difficulty of accepting hearsay evidence as against that of a witness who's given evidence live in court. Now, are there any other objections? Very well. We can now hear from Mr. Sweeney, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness comes in, may I address you on one -- actually, respond to one inquiry you made yesterday about some IC pictures that were taken about where the Sejdi Batusha house was on Exhibit P99, the aerial view of the village Mala Krusa. I would have the reference for you now. It is IC64 and IC65, and it is referred to by Mr. Ramadani in the transcript of 28 September, transcript page 4289 to 4290.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think Mr. Sweeney will need these just for the moment. We can rig them up in due course, I think. Good afternoon, Mr. Sweeney.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which is now being placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, it's probably as well you get fitted up with the earphones for later in the evidence. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Could you state your name for the transcript once more, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. It's John Sweeney.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And where are you from, Mr. Sweeney?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I'm from London. I work for the BBC now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And before I go any further, I may remind you what I was reminded of by the interpreters before the session, that we need to pause a little bit between question and answer for the purpose of translation into Serbian and other languages. Mr. Sweeney, you already stated your profession. How long have you been working in this position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I have been a reporter since 1977, too long, and in that time I've worked for a number of newspapers; the Observer newspaper for 12 years. And then towards the end of that time I was also doing films for Channel 4, dispatches, which is why I am here today. And since 2001, I have been working for the BBC.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how would you describe your -- what kind of journalist -- as what kind of journalist would you describe yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, in the sense --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: In terms of -- maybe I can lead a little bit. Would it be fair to say you're an investigative journalist?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Some people think I'm a terrible journalist, but others -- I'm an investigative journalist. I have won a number of awards when I was on the Observer, the UK Journalist of the Year. I've won prizes from Amnesty International for an investigation into torture in Chechnya. I've won television prizes for a massacre in Kosovo, for my reporting of that, and also for an investigation into miscarriages of justice in Britain. So I've won a series of awards. I'm currently the Paul Foot prize winner which is a prize in honour of an investigative journalist. So I am an investigative journalist and I have some track record.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you said already you won an award for a documentary regarding crimes committed in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously, this Court isn't about the quality of one's journalism, but I did -- in the spring and summer of 1999, I did two television documentaries along -- at the same time, I was writing articles for the Observer newspaper. And essentially it was the story of the massacre in little Krusa, in Albanian Krusha e Vogel, in Serbian Mala Krusa.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, did you give a statement to this Tribunal on the 22nd, 23rd, and 24th January, 2001?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you review this statement when you came here this week?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And do you attest that the statement accurately reflects your evidence and what you would say if examined today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender at this point Exhibit P2363 under seal, this is the unredacted version; and the redacted version, which is P2383.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You already told us a little bit about your experience. How many years did you work on issues related to the Balkans before you did the documentary about Mala Krusa?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I first went to what was Yugoslavia in 1991, after President Milosevic, as was, sent the tanks in against the students. That's around the spring -- certainly in the spring of 1991. I covered the sieges of Vukovar, Vinkovci, Osijek, Dubrovnik, the battle for Zagreb, the movements of people, refugees, killings of policemen initially and then refugees. In 1992, I covered the Balkan war from the summer onwards, and I made trips back in 1994, I believe, as well. I came back to the -- the region -- it's fair to say that I've covered the region from 1989, the revolution in Romania. I wrote a book about Ceaucescu. So, in all, I've been in the region for quite a while, and in Yugoslavia -- former Yugoslavia, in particular, from 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to talk to you about these two documentaries that you did about the events in Krusha e Vogel. The names of these documentaries are "Witness to Murder" and "Prime Suspect." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How did you first hear about Krusha e Vogel at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: What happened was that the whole world knew that there was -- there was great trouble brewing. There had been a series of killings in Kosovo, and most journalists, like myself, find it extremely difficult to get visas into Yugoslavia, into Serbia, and into Kosovo in particular. So I had come to Albania and was in -- my base was Tirana. I was trying to essentially get as close to what was going on. We heard very quickly NATO had dropped bombs on Belgrade, and we knew that there would be a reaction to this by the Serb authorities. There was. There was a river of refugees running from Kosovo into Albania, and so as soon as I practically could, myself and a couple of newspaper colleagues went to the border -- to as close as we could to the border to interview people. Basically what we were trying to do was to find out the most recent, the most fresh information. I wasn't working for Channel 4, the television company, at this time; I was just working for the Observer. And what happens is, as we're driving towards the border, essentially we're going sort of east back from Tirana to the border between Kosovo and Albania. We're driving the car and we see a group of, I would say, I don't know, five, six, seven men who were clearly exhausted, who got themselves by the side of the road, and they lay there and they looked shattered. We stopped the car, put the car in reverse, and we talked to them. They were, I believe -- I think they were the (redacted). But they were the men who had lived in little Krusa, but on the other side of the road from where most of the men and boys were killed, and they had managed to escape. Now, they said that some of their relatives had been killed and there had been a massacre in the village. How many? More than a hundred, they said. And I wrote it down in my notebook, little Krusa, Mala Krusa. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: -- it stuck in my mind to see if I could get to the bottom of this one. What happened subsequently was we got to the front line and we saw the general, sort of, scenes of chaos. But I thought now I'm going to try and find out about this massacre, about what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can I stop you here?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We have to move on. After you found out generally about this massacre, so-called massacre, had happened according to these people, did you then start to try to find some of the survivors in refugee camps in Albania, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. Let me --

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Sure thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: We have only limited time.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to cut you short a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: To how many of these refugee camps did you go, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: We trawled in Albania. We went to Elbasan, Fier, again and again and again. We'd heard -- by this time, I'd heard a story that there was a man who'd survived the massacre who'd run away, and he had burnt hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we play a short video-clip showing the situation in the camps in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: "JOHN SWEENEY: But there are so many claims of massacre. What's needed is hard evidence. We set out to uncover what really happened in just one small place. We set out to find someone who didn't just hear of the killing but saw it with their own eyes. We set out to name the killers. Albania, Europe's poorest country, has had to cope with an avalanche of humanity. Finding anyone from little Krusa, just a thousand souls in the chaos of half a million refugees, was not going to be easy. We are looking for people from Krusha e Vogel. We are looking for people from Krusha e Vogel. Yes, from Krusha e Vogel." "UNKNOWN MAN: We go there because they are telling us there are people ..." "JOHN SWEENEY: To help me I call up an old friend, the writer Agim Neza who knows his way around."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: "JOHN SWEENEY: But there are so many claims of massacre. What's needed is hard evidence. We set out to find out what really happened in just one small place. We set out to find someone who didn't just hear of the killing but saw it with their own ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, there has -- seems to have been a technical mistake. I think we're -- it was actually supposed to go on into the camp. I think we will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, where was that camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of -- it's difficult to tell precisely. We started off in Tirana, and we went to a good number around -- we found a woman who knew somebody from a neighbouring village, and we managed to pursue a family member to Elbasan, who was able to tell us more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you're misunderstanding my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm looking at the broader picture and trying to identify which particular camp this was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a camp, a refugee camp, on the outskirts of Tirana; that's where we started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the buildings we see in the film are part of Tirana.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's helpful to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure thing. We started from there and we sort of trawled through a number of refugee camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to try to replay it from the sequence where it suddenly jumped back because that shows the actual camp, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: "UNKNOWN MAN: We go there because they are telling us there are ..." "JOHN SWEENEY: To help me I call up an old friend, the writer Agim Neza, who knows his way around. Cruelty cannot be measured by numbers alone. Everyone here - doctors, peasants, teachers, labourers, and poets - has their own story of agony. It's hard to take in all this pain. But if we understood the horror of one war crime, it would help to understand the horror that is Kosovo. No one from little Krusa here."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, the other camps that you went to and tried to find survivors of the killing, was the situation for the refugees similar to the one we just saw in this clip?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes, yes. People were scattered, literally, across Albania, and the -- the story was the same. They had been chased out of their homes at gunpoint. They were afraid. There were some stories -- in a sense, we were focussing on Krusha e Vogel, but there was just a mountain of misery these people had run.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Okay. Approximately which time was it that you went to these refugee camps?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, immediately after the NATO bombing, so it's in, essentially, the week we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So April of 1999.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes, it's April 1999 -- well, it's late March and -- very late March and early April.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And for the first documentary, "Witness to Murder," you actually never got to go into Kosovo before this documentary was aired, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: No. We succeeded in finding, I think at the end, three witnesses - certainly we put, I think, three on film - who had been in the massacre, they said, and they had managed to run away and survive. We'd also spoken to a good number of the women folk who had witnessed the scenes running -- essentially the selection, what happened to the village before and after, and we used that evidence. We didn't say -- we didn't say we'd gone back to the village because that would have been wholly untrue. We were accurate and fair in saying that these are the stories that we hear from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you say that you talked to a number of people. Could you describe to the Court how you would interview the people you talked to about these events.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, what we tried to do, bearing in mind the chaos of this mass refugee -- with the chaos, the number of people that were running, what we tried to do was interview individual people on their own, as much as possible. There is an awful lot of, sort of, white noise of chaos. And I wanted to say to people: "No. Did you see with it your own eyes?" And I wanted to interview them, where best, person to person, so there's just myself, the translator, and the camera, and I wanted to find out who did it, who did they see -- in particular, the women, who did they see coming towards -- and, as far as possible, we tried to do that. Sometimes we failed; some of the time we succeeded. But we managed by focussing on this one particular thing, we managed to build up a clear picture of who we were looking for and who the key personalities in it were, and who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This first documentary, "Witness to Murder," was aired in Great Britain in May 1999 already?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And only after that point you then got to actually enter Kosovo, where you then made the second documentary, "Prime Suspects." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. Bear in mind, for a journalist like myself at this time, it was impossible for me to get a visa into Serbia because of the way Serbia, then Yugoslavia, was controlled, so that I wanted to go there but I couldn't. And it was only when NATO went in that we were -- had the occasion, from the 12th of June onwards, I went in, as it happens, on a British tank, hitched a lift. And a couple of days later, we drove down from Pristina down to the south-west corner --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: -- and that's when I got to little Krusa.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So you entered basically the day when UNMIK entered.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I entered the day that NATO -- well, whatever the name of the army, on the 12th of June, yes, that very first day, but I went to Pristina with the British army. A couple of journalists, German journalists, were killed, I think, that day or the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, Mr. Sweeney, we cannot hear all the details today.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Sure thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You already mentioned you went from Pristina down to Krusha e Vogel. What did you notice on your way there? How was the state of the villages you came by?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: There was an astonishing, obvious discrepancy. Albanian homes had been burnt; Serb homes were untouched. There had been NATO bombing, and when I saw a couple of the big TV -- I think a TV mast in Pristina had got hit, but the hits by NATO were very, very precise. The rest of the countryside, you could go through a Serbian village and the routes were untouched. Now, that changed later when there was some Albanian payback on the Serbs, but at the time I was first there, it was self-evident. You knew you were in a village with Albanian homes because they'd been burnt down, the route had gone, the people had fled, and you'd see animals, cows, dogs, running around. And this general -- without their owners. And this general picture was certainly the case in Krusa -- in little Krusa.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And which villages or cities did you come by while you were in Kosovo where you noticed the kind of destruction that you just described, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: It was -- the destruction got worse the closer you went west, the more -- in a sense, I think there was an attempt by the Serb military and police to close down the possibility of any support for the people they would see as the guerillas, the UCK, from Albania --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you again, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the witness giving his thoughts about an attempt by Serb military and police to do things he doesn't know about. He doesn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Sweeney, you should confine yourself to answering the particular questions that are asked of you --?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- because there are contentious issues that we know about which may not be the uppermost in your mind but which the court has to be alert to. That is why counsel are themselves trying to control the questions they ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. It's fair to say that there was much more damage done to homes in the west of the country --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had that answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- so let's move on to the next question, please, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: On which day did you enter Krusha e Vogel, if you remember? Just the date.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I think it was the 14th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we play the next video which shows the village at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "JOHN SWEENEY: It's mid-June. The war is over. Powers of the NATO rolls into Kosovo. I'm close on their heels. The Serb forces are retreating, but liberation comes too late for 10.000 murdered Albanians. Krusha e Vogel? Krusha e Vogel? Our murder inquiry starts at the scene of the crime. This is little Krusa, a ruin of a village in a ruin of a country. You can't get to the bottom of 10.000 murders; you can try with a hundred. Little Krusa is empty, abandoned, yet full of ghosts. This is the aftermath of ethnic cleansing."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How many of the houses in Krusha e Vogel looked like the ones depicted in the documentary?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Most of them, most of them, the majority -- a certain number of the village, most of them had been gutted. The ones which weren't, we found, were the ones who'd belonged to the Serbs who fled. By the time we got back, most of the Albanians -- the Kosovars who were in the refugee camps hadn't returned, so we, in fact, got there before they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And close to your arrival in Krusha e Vogel, you also tried to find the Batusha hay-barn or cow-shed in which the killing had allegedly taken place.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: It was unrecognisable. Your Honour, bear in mind that all our descriptions had come from the refugees, and they were -- they were talking about the time -- they were advising us about the time. They didn't know that their homes had been burnt. I think they'd seen smoke in the distance, but they weren't sure. We were looking for a hay-barn and couldn't find it at first. Then one of the villagers showed us. When we arrived it was a hole in the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And we are going to play the next clip which will show this sequence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: "JOHN SWEENEY: The trail of evidence begins with a hay-barn, but where is it? The village is full of gutted hay barns. One of the first refugees to return is someone who'd actually survived the machine-gunning. Everything he owned is ashes, and that is not the worst of it. Shamil Shehu lost 40 members of his family. He knows exactly where the hay-barn is. The last time Shamil had taken this path, he had been forced at gunpoint along with 111 men of his village. The hay-barn isn't here anymore; instead, just a crater. No bullets. No blood. No bodies. The Serbs had blown it up." "SHAMIL SHEHU: I still find it hard to believe that I'm alive. I wish that they'd killed me rather than my sons. Here I lost two of my sons, three brothers, and five nephews. Altogether, 40 of my family were killed. Now I have to look after what's left of my family." "JOHN SWEENEY: This man, Rasim Batusha, is the owner of the hay-barn. He's alive because he was away working on a building site in Germany. Now everything is gone. Twenty-two of Rasim's relatives were murdered here, among them, his three brothers and his eldest son." "RASIM BATUSHA: I found this over there in the middle of that pit. It can't be anything else but a human bone."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: So just for us to understand, in June 1999, when you first came to the site where the hay-barn had been, was one of the holes actually not yet filled with water?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. Those pictures are taken from the very earliest time, I think, so if there's no water in it, there was no water at the time. Let's remember, if it rains a lot, it's going to fill up and go. We were there quite a while, but I think those were some of the very first pictures we took.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the bone was found in the ditch that was filled with water or in the other one, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I can't recall where it was found. I didn't find it. I don't know whether that's a human bone or not. In a sense, we're reporting their suspicions. What they're trying to do is find their relatives. They're trying to find bones; they're trying to find bodies. They think they're dead and they couldn't find them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the next step in your investigation in this matter was that you started searching in some of the abandoned Serbian houses in the village, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. We were worried lest they be booby-trapped, but it struck me -- we'd got a series of names from the Albanians, the people -- that the women had eye-witnessed basically back in -- a couple of months before that. They had seen their neighbours; they identified them. Dmitri Nikolic was one name; Savo Nikolic was another.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: And I went to their homes to look for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we play the next clip, please, that shows this. [Videotape played]. "JOHN SWEENEY: Our third break. The Serbs were outnumbered ten to one in Kosovo. They were the ones with the fire power. Nearly every Serb man and boy in the village was armed and mobilised in the local militia. The Serb militia were careless. They left this behind. It looks like a scruffy exercise book, but it's material evidence. In it are a series of names of soldiers who were on guard in little Krusa after the massacre. Amongst the names are two that are becoming all too familiar - Sveta Tasic and Sava Nikolic. And there is another find - a duty rota, another item of material evidence. It's astonishing they've left this behind. This list identifies 24 names, making up three militia platoons in little Krusa. Some we know have form. The document places all 24 men on militia duty in the village. All of these men know something about the clean-up operation. Some of them know something about the murders. All are suspects now."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The notebook and the list of names that were just shown in this clip, did you find both items yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't find the notebook, which is the first document. That was handed to me by one of the Albanian women. The second document I believe I found myself. It's hard to remember this far back, but I was talking to my colleague, the producer, and he said, "No, John, you found nearly everything in there," because it almost became a mission of mine to find the evidence, anything we could. I was also looking for photographs so we could put images to names. So I found the second piece of paper, I believe, but the notebook was handed to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, where are these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they are with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. They're now in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are they exhibits in the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: They are, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You just referred to having found photographs as well. Once you had these photographs, did you meet up with some of the survivors who had at that point returned to the village to identify the persons on the photos?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how did you do this procedure?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, what we wanted to do was to be absolutely sure -- let's remember that this is -- there isn't a more serious allegation you can make against someone that they've taken part in a massacre. So we wanted to be absolutely sure that we had a correct match between the photo and the name. So I think we did this process several times, but we also -- we filmed -- we filmed it with two of our key Albanian witnesses from the village. Let's bear in mind, by the way, that this village had been -- was half and half, Albanian and Serb, so everybody knew everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we play the next clip which depicts this identification procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: "JOHN SWEENEY: I'd taken a pile of photographs from the Serbs' houses. I began with a list of four suspects. Now I've got 24. But are any of these mug shots of the men I am looking for? The next step is to get Mehmet and Shamil together to identify the line-up." "SHAMIL SHEHU: He was the first to shoot at us. As our families were heading for the mountains, Sava shot at us from his house." "JOHN SWEENEY: Now we can put faces to names: Sava Nikolic; his comrade in arms, Sveta Tasic; their friend and neighbour, Momcilo Nikolic, and his uncle Dmitri Nikolic. Now we know what the men on our wanted list look like. We can start to track them down."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair to say that you had already been in the village for some time before the exhumation team for the ICTY ever arrived there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. They -- I'm not sure when they turned up, but we'd been there for a -- for about a month, I think, but certainly two or three weeks before they turned up. They had other work to do, so it's not as if they were being lazy. It was just that -- but this place was our priority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, who was the person who referred to being shot at in the last clip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That man is -- is that Mehmet Shehu? No, that's Shamil; that's his first name. What he's referring to, Your Honour, is that there was a day when the Serb forces first arrived, the Serb forces and their neighbours, chased the villagers -- or the villagers ran off into the hills, and I believe that Sava Nikolic shot at them -- or his testimony is referring to that man, or what he's saying is referring to that moment. And they came back the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please bear in mind my question again. It was just simply the identification of the person I was after. It's important you confine yourself to answering the questions that are asked because of the time constraints that are on us. It gets very boring referring to these, but they are important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered it. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shamil Shehu, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. And the second person you've already mentioned, Mehmet, the second person that was sitting there with you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: That's Mehmet Krasniqi, who, in my deposition -- you can answer that point, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I think the Court is familiar with this name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we are approaching the time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How long is your examination going to be, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I have -- I have three more clips that I would like to play and ask some questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- so maybe another 10 to 12 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll resume at ten minutes past 4.00. Mr. Sweeney, the usher will show you where to wait while we have our break. If you can just leave the courtroom just now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before we continue, Mr. Sweeney, you said that this was a village where the population was about 50/50, Serb/Albanian. We've had evidence already from eye-witnesses to this incident, including Mehmet, now Krasniqi, but you may have known him as Avdyli, who said that it had a minority Serb population. There were only about a quarter of the number of houses -- sorry, in fact, he said there were only about 23 Serb houses, yes, and about a hundred Albanian houses. You had a different impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm wrong. It's his village. Geographically there was a kind of -- a small part of the village where the massacre took place where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't need to know any more than that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- If you accept that he's more likely to be correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He lives there; I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Second question I would like to ask you: We saw these two documents, the book and the document. To what organisation did they relate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. My guess -- my educated guess was that it was some kind of a duty rota.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but anyway, you don't know the answer to what organisation they relate. And my third question is: What happened to the uniform that you showed on the video-clip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We -- that would have been left there. Essentially we went into these places, filmed them, and then left. The exception -- the things that I took from the places, the Serb homes, were passbooks and photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And just picking up on the uniform issue, was that the only uniform you saw in this house, or did you find uniforms in several houses or in any other house?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I believe I found -- there were sort of militia uniforms or police or army uniform in a number of houses. It's difficult to remember at this distance, but yes -- it wasn't a surprise. It was just -- it was a nice shot of one uniform. I'm sure I saw others.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Do you recall how the others you saw looked like?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I would hesitate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not surprisingly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- because you don't remember, as far as I can tell from this end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We left off before the break talking about the exhumation team arriving in Krusha e Vogel, and I would like to play the next short clip, which is two short consecutive clips. Your team actually filmed part of this procedure, did it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: "JOHN SWEENEY: Two months after the end of the war, forensic experts from Scotland Yard arrive in little Krusa. They are working for the war crimes tribunal at The Hague, but they've been busy. There are 10.000 murders to solve in Kosovo. Their task is to find out who was killed and how. There is precious little for them to do at the hay-barn, so they are probing what's left of this second murder site in the village."

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: "JOHN SWEENEY: This is all that remains of six men. Shot in the back and burned in yet another war crime. The relatives of the 106 men murdered in the hay-barn haven't got even this grim consolation. Unidentified bones and other debris have been found by the river Drin. All the clues point to this as the place where the victims of the hay-barn murder were dumped."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This lorry that we just saw on the River Drin, did you investigate that any further?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. I went for a swim.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you had a closer look at that one, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes, I swam down to it. It was in a difficult position to get the camera around. But I swam around and saw what I believed to be bloodstains.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we play the next two short clips on this, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: "JOHN SWEENEY: So, there's a tarpaulin lorry. It's empty, but this looks like lots and lots of blood on the lorry."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: "JOHN SWEENEY: Okay, so, um ..." "CAMERAMAN: Is there anything?" "UNKNOWN WOMAN: Are there still bloodstains over there?" "JOHN SWEENEY: Sorry?" "UNKNOWN WOMAN: Bloodstains." "JOHN SWEENEY: Yeah, there's -- there's -- it's absolutely soaked in blood."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the exhumation team ever had a look at this lorry?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I don't believe they did. I can remember trying at the time to get NATO to fish it out, but they were -- I believe they were very busy. But I don't believe anybody has got, sort of, images of that. The camera angle -- essentially, the bloodstains were on the river side, so we couldn't get our camera at it. We didn't use that clip in our film, for whatever reason, but I -- it's bringing it back to me and I can remember there was what looked to me like a lot of bloodstains.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this exhibit has its own number because it's a small excerpt from the raw material that we do not seek to tender. It's Exhibit Number P2364.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to it. It shows nothing but Mr. Sweeney going for a swim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the practice we follow here, Mr. Ackerman, is that these exhibits that are used in court are there to illustrate what was shown, and the only way we can know that's all it shows is to have it in the process. So it is admitted under our practice, but that doesn't carry with it any other implication than that it will be evaluated for what it shows. So, carry on, please, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you some more questions in relation to your statement. You speak about having seen -- in June 1999, having seen mass destruction of Albanian homes and shops inside Kosovo. Do you remember any villages or cities where you saw that? And only give us the name, if you can.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: The damage -- the serious damage, the kind of -- where almost not a home was missed, would be on the west side; towns like Gjakova, all the villages down from Gjakova to Krusha e Vogel. And there was a strange -- it stopped around Prizren. So, for whatever reason, there wasn't violence, there wasn't evidence of arson of Albanian homes, roofless, gutted, burnt down around there; but going north up that road, there was. So virtually all the villages -- certainly the village greater Krusa was damaged. I believe that 20 people killed there. And on to Gjakova. Those are the places I can be absolutely certain of. But we're talking about the destruction of almost every single Albanian home. And then you'd pass through a Serbian area and the homes would be untouched at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how would you know at that time which area was Albanian and which was Serbian?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, almost -- almost because you could -- whether they -- they had a roof on their homes or not. This is what people told us. But essentially the stories became -- it became obvious that it was true. And certainly my experience of both little and greater Krusa, which I knew in some detail, it was clear that all of the Albanian homes had been -- or nearly all of them had been burnt -- burnt and destroyed. And the wreckage was devastating.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And another point I wish to clarify in your statement. It's on page 9, the second-last paragraph. Therein you say that from March 1999 you saw hundreds of thousands of ethnic Albanian refugees displaced from their homes at gunpoint. I wish to clarify what you meant to say by that, because you weren't in Kosovo at that time, I understood.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. No, it's poor use of English. They told me that they had -- that they had fled. What I saw was a stream of refugees, hundreds of thousands of them - myself and many other people, journalists, aid workers, people from the UN, and so forth - a constant river of humanity, trucks -- a few trucks, mainly tractors, on foot, mothers, old people, screaming -- all saying the same story, that they'd been pursued by the Serbs, they'd been told to go, to fuck off to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, you were also given a home video by the Batusha family, if I understand correctly, showing men and boys that were killed in the killing in the Batusha barn, when they were still alive at a wedding. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. It's a simple thing lots of families would have everywhere in the world. It's a video of their wedding party.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could we play this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: "JOHN SWEENEY: Rasim, granny Batusha's eldest son, is the only man left in the family. He has given up his job in Germany and come to look after the wives and children of his dead brothers. He brought the only record left of the men of little Krusa - the video of the wedding party of his murdered son Agi."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The women and children that you see in this clip, who were they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: They're members of the Batusha family. I first met them in Albania, in April, and essentially by this time they were -- they'd realised that their men had been killed. They knew that pretty much. They didn't see their men being killed. They were very much part of the selection; they were the people who were put to one side. Then their men trooped off - this is what they told me - and then they heard the machine-gun fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would complete my questions. Would you like me to tender the exhibits now or at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we know what exhibits you've actually used, but I need to find out from Mr. Sweeney a little more about the two video films that were broadcast in 1999. What, on these, have we not seen that will help us to determine what happened and who was responsible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to -- hard for me to give a short answer to that, but basically we tried quite hard to be as correct and as dispassionate about the evidence that we got. The survivors of the massacre in the film -- or the survivors, in particular the women, identify the people who were at the selection. And then we have the men who climbed from underneath the dead bodies and ran away. There is one particular image which sticks in my mind which made me understand what took place and -- well, it's -- in fact, some of the survival testimony. The man with burnt hands, Mehmet Krasniqi, he's holding his hands behind his back, and there's a moment where he ducks before the machine-gun fire. And that's why he got to the ground. And then he was covered with the people who had been mortally wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's helpful for you to tell us that, but bear in mind we've seen him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you've seen him. You've seen him in a courtroom some years after the event. We filmed him at the -- well, within a month or two of it happening. But I wouldn't want to, in any way -- to tell you to watch this film. You're Judges; you're wholly capable of making up your own mind about the evidence. All I can say is that there are a number of scenes in the film which we found compelling. Now, we may have got little bits and pieces wrong, but we found the picture we told compelling of the hundred-plus men and boys taken to the hay-barn, a tiny number of survivors. The women are witnesses to it, and they know at least some of the people who did that, because they recognise their neighbours, bearing in mind they also said that the army and the police were there, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, what do you maintain that viewing the rest of these films would add factually to our knowledge and enable us to determine what happened and who was responsible?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I think it would -- as I already said, it contains a lot of -- which would be hearsay evidence, of course, of other persons talking about the events, the females who were concerned by these events. It also contains extensive footage showing the two witnesses who testified here and who talked about the same event in a contemporaneous manner, very close after the events occurred, which would corroborate their testimony they gave here and the exact nature. It would also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One person giving an account on two occasions can't be corroboration; it's the same source of evidence, the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, but what I tried to say is it would demonstrate that the recollection of the witnesses when testifying here was still very clear and vivid, as the accounts are so identical that were given on both occasions. It does also show some more visual documentary evidence about -- the second video, which was filmed in Kosovo, gives some more visual evidence about the situation in around Mala Krusa at the time, in June 1999, as it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, this is not a matter for you now, Mr. Sweeney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. We have decided that we will admit these two video films in their entirety but are particularly conscious of the fact that anything said by an apparent eye-witness to these events will be regarded as hearsay which has not been subject to cross-examination. Mr. O'Sullivan. Sorry. Judge Chowhan has a question before we ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I apologise to the counsel for this. Well, I just want to understand your personality, because it's essential that we know about a witness. Now, for that, I had two names before me of journalists, to find out which one of them you go along with: Is it Walter Lippman or is it Phillip Simpson -- John Simpson? Just to understand how you persevere. Or do you go for men like Domenico Lapar [phoen] or things like that? They're all historical. Yes, some more like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would -- I would go for a different set of names, and the key name is the man whose name escapes me right now, who is the American reporter Murrow, Ed Murrow, who fought against McCarthy-ism. I admire all of the people you've named. I think some of the people I'm not sure about. I would seek to have done my best. One of the things I think I'm quite proud of, as a programme team, was that after we'd been in the village about two months, the Albanians burnt down the Serb homes. Remember, the Serbs had done. But we show that in the documentary. So the point is -- I'd like to make, is that this isn't -- we didn't set out to make propaganda; we set out to try and find out what had happened. And so when the Albanians burnt down the homes of their Serb neighbours, albeit that the Serb neighbours had gone, we showed that, too. So I think it's very important for a journalist, when they come across inconvenient truths, to report those, too. Those are the kinds of journalists I admire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The order will be: General Pavkovic, General Ojdanic, General Lazarevic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, and General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sweeney.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right at the beginning of your testimony, you said there were some people who think you're a terrible journalist. Why would someone think you're a terrible journalist?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: It was a joke.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, it was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, okay. We were provided with a bunch of documents that you apparently gave to the Prosecution, which they then gave to us, a number of things that you have written, and I wanted to talk to you just a little bit about some of those things. Before I do that, I want to ask you something else, though. You're now working with BBC?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And is there any particular project you're working on now?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: No -- well, I've just finished a film which aired concerns about David Mills, his relationship with Silvio Berlusconi, and his wife or estranged wife's business/personal conduct as well. She is the Secretary of State for Culture. That was a BBC panorama piece that was aired on Sunday. I am now waiting for the next thing I'm supposed to be doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you been doing anything with regard to, for instance, Iraq or Lebanon or any of the more recent conflicts?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I have to say that the cameraman, James Miller, who shot the second film was killed by an Israeli soldier in 2003, and almost as a direct result of that death, I have pretty much ceased to go to war zones. I did spend -- I was actually in Iraq when I heard about James' death; I spent a month in 2003 in Iraq. But since then I haven't been anywhere that people would consider a war zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go back to these documents. The first one I want to talk about is a letter -- it looks like a letter; it may not be. It may be a message of some kind. It says: "From John Sweeney to Paul Vickers, 8 July 1999," and it was something you were writing to him. And what you said in that was: "The war in Kosovo has changed the way the democracies will fight battles forever. The tyrant of Belgrade was humiliated and not a single soldier or airman was lost in the battle, even though NATO, despite the bluster, only hit 13 tanks." You mention the bluster of NATO. What do you mean when you speak of the bluster of NATO?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, there was a -- well, first of all, I'm not quite sure, unless I see it, what that was. Paul Vickers is a friend of mine. Was this something that I had written for a newspaper or for the BBC, or am I e-mailing a friend? That's my first point. Second point: NATO, for many of us on the ground, we saw, had been aware of a stream of violence coming out of Belgrade from 1991 onwards, to do -- driven by Slobodan Milosevic, and there was -- certainly as far as most of my fellow journalists were concerned, there was an annoyance that NATO sort of said, We'll have air cover, air support. It didn't actually stop the wars happening in Bosnia and in Kosovo. So that's what I meant by "bluster."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And then you talk about NATO only hitting 13 tanks. To your knowledge, today, the knowledge you have today, is that an accurate figure?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: At this distance, I wouldn't want to stand by it.
