Certainly I've been to Belgrade since then, I think sometime in 1999 or 2000, and obviously -- no, the 13 tanks was a story at the time, so I think it was roughly accurate. That's what people were saying at the time. If we know better now, then fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you know, don't you, that NATO had Predator drone-surveillance kinds of aircraft operating over Kosovo; they had other kinds of surveillance aircraft; they had A-10 warthog tank-killer aircraft. You know about all that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: The people who were running the predators weren't advertising that in 1999. Certainly, if this was written on the 8th of July, 1999, I wouldn't have known all that detail. I was aware of the stuff -- one was aware of it. I didn't see any predator drones. So your question is -- well, I don't quite see what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what I'm getting at is, if this figure is correct, this 13 tanks, with all of the air power and capability that NATO had at the time, would you agree that only 13 tanks were hit because the tanks must have been kept very well hidden from NATO air cover?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, what you're asking me to defend is -- if I understand it correctly, it's an e-mail to a friend --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm really not asking you to defend anything. I'm asking you for what knowledge you might have.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know you went to a lot of NATO briefings, so I know you were familiar with what NATO was doing.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I think I went to -- because I was on the ground, you couldn't -- and I think I only went to one -- I did one trip to NATO Brussels headquarters, where I was very sceptical of what NATO was saying because I had seen the performance on the ground. I believe that they must have hit more than 13 tanks, because subsequently we learnt more about what they did. There was -- NATO said publicly, "We do not want to hit civilians," and there were a number of atrocities which were blamed on NATO, and I investigated two of them. These were strikes against tractors. Obviously this is more than 13 tanks. Those very stories -- that one had real doubts about what really had happened. I can go on, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I think that's good enough. What I do want to tell you is, if I mention any document that you would like to look at before you answer, if you let me know, I can get it brought over to you, because I have them all here.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: For example, if we're going to talk about this some more, then you should show me a copy of this, whatever it was, e-mail, to my friend Paul Vickers. But I would say that I'm not the NATO high commander. Basically I'm a reporter who spent a lot of time in little Krusa, from June 1999 onwards. I mean, not a huge amount of time, but I spent every day there for about four weeks, spread over six weeks, having been informed by the survivors of the massacre in late April -- late March/early April of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the same e-mail - and, again, I'll show it to you if you want to see it - in the same e-mail, you speak of a journalist by the name of John Pilger. Is that the way you pronounce his name?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you say that he denounced your reporting from his gilded south London salon.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'd stick by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you know John Pilger well, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I know of him. He was a man I used to admire. But the problem is that he was denouncing my journalism about what had happened and he hadn't been to Kosovo. He hadn't been before or he hadn't been after. And there is a certain point to which, if you're a reporter, you report what you see on the ground. And if somebody in London says, "This is rubbish, this is not true," then you -- one reacts quite -- it's annoying, because how does he know, if he's in London, what's going on in, say, little Krusa?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You started your testimony today by -- I guess what you were trying to do was tell the Chamber that you were an accomplished and believable journalist by telling us the awards that you had won. John Pilger was, according to a document I have here, Descriptive Writer of the Year, 1966; Reporter of the Year, 1967 --

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I was at school then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- Journalist of the Year, 1967; International Reporter of the Year, 1970; New Reporter of the Year, 1974; Campaigning Journalist of the Year, 1977; Journalist of the Year, 1979; United Nations Media Peace Prize, Australia, 1979 and 1980; United Nations Media Peace Prize, Gold Medal, Australia, 1980, 1981 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, this is not a place for determining the relative worths of journalists. If there are material pieces of evidence that this witness has given that you want to challenge, then it would be helpful to have our attention drawn to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is just a round-about way of getting there. But if you don't want me to get there, you tell me. I mean, you're the Judge, and if you don't want me to get there this way, then I won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but it follows on from a statement that the witness made about another journalist. And if you're going to put something that Pilger has said that you think is relevant, fine; but if you're not going to do that by going through the history of his biography, it's not really going to enlighten us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree. It would be silly to be doing this if I wasn't going somewhere with it. I'm not just trying to make Pilger look good for the world. I'm going somewhere with it and I have something that he said that I want to use with this witness. Advise me what you'd like me to do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'd like you to ask the question that you want to ask, rather than go through a catalogue of his biography.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, then, can I come back to his biography, so you will understand that we're dealing with a very reputable journalist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If it turns out to be relevant. But just because he's a reputable -- I suspect you will get the witness to agree that's he's regarded as a reputable journalist, but perhaps not by him now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have his books on my bookshelf. He wrote about me once in an admiring way and that was great. I never saw him in Yugoslavia, not once.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now he's answering a question I didn't even ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's get to the question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The point is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, please, Mr. Sweeney, let's just get to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. I'm trying to guess it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going back to your letter to John Sweeney or your e-mail --

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I'm John Sweeney.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, to Paul Vickers. You say to Paul Vickers: "Under the immense pressure to get access, any access to the war, I would argue rigorous journalism collapsed." Does that mean that there was a great deal of unreliable journalism coming out of the war in Kosovo? Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: There was a lot of pressure to work out what was going on, and it was very, very difficult. Everything's difficult in a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us today - and it's also in your statement - that one of the things that makes you comfortable about the conclusions you drew about what happened in Mala Krusa was the similarity of the statements that you heard from people that had been there at the time.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I don't think I used the word "comfortable."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You probably didn't. That's my word. Are you uncomfortable about it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was something that was decisive in letting you draw the conclusions that you drew, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I have another document here that was written by you, and I don't know how to identify it to you. At the very top it just has: "John Sweeney, Skopije."

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You speak of a person by the name of Audrey Gillen, and I'll show it to you if you want to see it. Let me tell you what you said there, and then if you want to check that, you can. You said with regard to Audrey Gillen's challenge: "What's the story? She is right to be uneasy of the near uniformity of the refugees' claims. She is right to be uneasy about the power of hysteria and the power of propaganda by the Kosovo Liberation Army."

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I'd stick with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. What do you mean when you talk there about the power of hysteria?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: People -- this isn't the first massacre story that I've done, so I've been to a number of places where terrible things have happened: Chechnya, Iraq, Burundi, Algeria. And there is a fear of speaking openly; there is a fear of evidence-gathering, often because there is malevolent, secret police, there is no proper free media. That's the kind of environment we're dealing with, and so you have to sift evidence. And I believe Audrey Gillen was a journalist for The Guardian and she wrote a piece, sort of saying: There is a problem with the refugees; they're all saying the same thing. But the problem is we couldn't go, certainly I couldn't go, into Yugoslavia and see for myself because of the nature of the regime there - police controls, police checks. And basically, if you weren't a sympathetic journalist, you couldn't get inside Yugoslavia at the time. So we've got a problem with the people telling us the story; we can't go and check it out. That's why I was very keen to get to little Krusa as fast as possible and check out this story and see for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, but I asked you about the word "hysteria." You used the words "the power of hysteria" and I want to know what you meant by that. I know you couldn't go check out the story right then.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Right, but it means that people who are afraid are sometimes not careful, not precise, about what's happened to them. They just say, for example, the Serbs have killed all our men. Now, for example, in little Krusa, that's not literally true but it's a quick, brief shouted remark on a hillside in Albania. It's not miles away from the truth. A hundred men, they said, men and boys, were killed. What's the exact number? We don't know. And I believe the latest number is something like 103. It's not far off. But there is a difference. There is a general point that I made -- was seeking to make there, that yes, there is hysteria in war and then there is a specific piece of evidence or bits of evidence that you find on the ground. So, in the general environment, where, as we know, in war, truth is the first casualty, that's the environment I'm looking at. That's, in a sense, what I'm used to dealing with. That doesn't mean that everything you hear from people is untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber what it is you know about the power of propaganda by the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the KLA was -- it was the army fighting for the ethnic Albanians in Kosovo, capable of murdering innocent people, of burning down Serb houses; that it was pretty ruthless. It didn't have much of a visible presence in little Krusa. In fact, one of the sad ironies of that village was that Serbs and Albanians had lived peacefully together for a long, long time. My understanding - I may be wrong about that - but that's what I was told. In other -- so when somebody in a KLA uniform would say something to me, I'd be skeptical. I'm a reporter; it's my job to be skeptical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go to another document now. This one is -- at the top it says: "John Sweeney," and then in bold it says: "NATO HQ."

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: This would -- I think, to set the scene for the Court, these are a series of articles I would have written for The Observer newspaper while, at the same time, I was making these two films.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. In this document you talk about the mistaken bombing by NATO of KLA army barracks where seven KLA were killed and 20 were wounded. You seem to indicate that this could not have been a mistake, since these barracks were the most well-publicised KLA position in the region, visited by several western journalists, including Euan Ferguson of The Observer. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, that's my article. I'm sure -- I would hope it was as correct as I could make it. It's clear from the article that I wasn't there. What I'm -- as we say, I'm sourcing it, I'm sourcing it to people who were there. I remember the story vaguely. I'm not an expert on this, but if I reported that, I'll stand by that report as being correct, as I knew it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, this shows your skepticism that you just talked about, I think, doesn't it? What you're saying is: I'm really skeptical about this being a mistake because this was a well-known KLA barracks.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm here, I believe, to give evidence about little Krusa, so I'm not quite sure where we're going. My point would be that, on little Krusa, I would consider myself to be something of an expert; on this, I don't know. I wasn't there. But I reported it at the time. What's the date of the article?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It doesn't have a date.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: It would have had a date. The question is, if this was the time period before NATO got in, some kind of free speech and free inquiry was possible after June 12th. Before that time, it was very difficult to find out what was going on. But if Euan Ferguson, who was a friend of mine and a colleague on The Observer, had been there, then I would have been reflecting his reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Now that you're here --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- it's open to counsel to ask you questions about anything on which they think you can give answers relevant to the issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your evidence is not confined to Mala Krusa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The transcript just died for all of us, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I see one, two, three, four, five. But I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that same piece, if that's what it is, you have written this: "NATO has kept the KLA at arm's length throughout the conflict, but killing seven of its troops is probably taking that diplomatic nicety too far." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Again, I haven't seen this article for a long, long time, so it would be useful if I could see it. I think I could work out the date of it, if you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If the usher could come get it and take it to you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Thanks very much. Basically it means -- it slightly means what it says, that NATO was -- as I understand it, was keen to not be fighting the KLA's war for it; that NATO had its own agenda, which was that of Western government, the Western public, the Western world, that they didn't like mass killing taking place in parts of Europe, and they didn't want to be alongside the KLA. However, I'm sure there was some information exchange; espionage, intelligence, whatever, what have you. I was aware of some of this going on. Killing seven members of the KLA in a well-known KLA position would have been a clear mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the impression I get from that sentence is that what you're saying is, NATO deliberately killed some KLA just to squelch any concerns that they might be working with them.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: No, I think that's a little -- no, I think that's taking it too far. The sense of the -- by the way, this -- I'm looking at here four or five paragraphs from an article with headline "NATO HQ." With no date on it, it's difficult for me to figure out whether it's a short article or whether it's part of a long article. I don't know. To answer your question, what was I was saying was I was making the following points, I believe: One, NATO has kept the KLA at arm's length throughout the conflict; true. "Killing seven troops is probably taking that diplomatic nicety too far" is making the point that, having made this mistake, it's embarrassing. It is true to say, obviously, that if NATO was fighting the Yugoslav army and Yugoslav police and the KLA are fighting it, then the two sides have got a degree of common interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the last paragraph there that I read to you, because you got it and I can't read it now --

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- any reader that concluded, like I did, that what you're saying is that NATO deliberately killed KLA just to squelch concerns that they might working with them, any reader that would conclude that would be justified in drawing that conclusion, I think, don't you? Even though that may not have been what you meant.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: If I read the article, then it's up to me -- I proclaim my right to defend what I meant by the article, not what you take to mean by the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's just not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I'm afraid this is not enlightening us one little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll leave it alone. If I can have my document back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, sure thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember writing an article, along with Jens Holst and Ed Vulliamy, dated Sunday, October 17th, 1999, regarding the NATO bombing of the Chinese embassy in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any memory today how many people were killed in the bombing of the Chinese embassy in Belgrade or in the attack on the embassy?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: It was a small number of people. From memory -- I haven't read that article for ages. I believe the Chinese -- it was about two or three Chinese and one or two locals. But the significance of the story was that I was skeptical -- all three of us were skeptical of NATO's official line that it was a mistake. I can explain more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Both NATO and the United States authorities explained that it was a mistake because of an outdated map, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. We found that -- well, what we got hold of, people inside the intelligence community, a serving soldier -- I don't want to blow my sources, but a serving soldier who is a signals bloke and somebody else who knows about how British intelligence works, and two separate sources said, "That's nonsense. They hit the embassy." Now, I went to the embassy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on there, please, Mr. Sweeney. Relevance of this, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's relevant to future testimony we're going to have from representatives of NATO regarding the precision of their bombing and the -- and it just goes to the credibility of the reports that we're going to get about what NATO was doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we really need to know more about the source of this witness's knowledge of this before it could have any real bearing on your assessment of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you -- and you can see this article again, if you'd like to see it. What you wrote here is: "NATO deliberately bombed the Chinese embassy in Belgrade during the war in Kosovo after discovering that it was being used to transmit Yugoslav army communications." And then you say: "According to sources in Europe and the US, the Chinese embassy was removed from a prohibited targets list after NATO electronic intelligence detected it sending army signals to Milosevic's forces." You apparently spoke to a Chinese embassy spokesman in London who said: "We don't believe that the embassy was bombed because of a mistake with an out-of-date map." Now, my question to you: Was this a totally reckless article on your part, or did you have a basis for this article?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: We had a basis for this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: As I said, I don't want to give away my sources, but we heard from credible people -- remember, that there are three names, so we went to some length to check it out, that they hadn't -- that the idea that they'd used a street map to identify the Chinese embassy was incredible. And my sources -- our sources told us - our sources told us - that they had an exact knowledge of where the Chinese embassy was. Now, the American government denied this story. The British foreign secretary -- I put it to him at a drinks party much, much later, and he didn't make a strong denial of the story, which always struck me as very interesting. I'm talking about the late Robin Cook. Until China opens up, we'll never know what really happened. But we had strong sources for this story.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. On May 18th, 1999, you talk about John Pilger. You say, in a writing that has basically your letterhead, I think, on it: "When John Pilger condemns British journalists for lickspittle reporting of the NATO war machine, one pauses for thought. Pilger attacked the Western media for failing to report NATO's savagery. He didn't quote a single Kosovar refugee. Pilger said: 'There is no sense of the revulsions felt throughout most of the world for this wholly illegal action for the punishment --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down when reading, please. Please read slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "-- for the punishment of Milosevic's crime with the greater crime." Was he criticising you for lickspittle reporting at that point? Were you specifically criticised?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, one of the things you have attempted to do - and I don't know what the status of it is - with regard to the investigation you did in Mala Krusa was to make a book out of it and sell that book. Have you had any success in selling your book?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: No. I'm a journalist. Every now and then one wants to write a book about something you know about. I believe that most Western publishers weren't -- publishers in Britain weren't interested in the story. Too much grief from the Balkans. I think -- I'd forgotten I intended to write a book. But it's happened before; it will happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you submitted it to, apparently, more than one publisher, submitted not the book but a proposal for a book, and one of the things we've been given is a -- I don't know what you call it. It has a big headline: "The Machine-Gunner was Running Late," by John Sweeney, and in it you describe the book you wanted to have published and the things you found in Mala Krusa that you thought were significant and sensational enough to justify the publication of a book. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I wouldn't have used the word "sensational."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I guess you'll agree with me that the more sensational you could make the story, the more likely it was that you would be able to make a book out of it. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I repeat my earlier answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you know, on page 4 of this -- of this thing you are trying to promote, this book you're trying to promote, you speak of Sava Nikolic and you say this: "Sava's passport shows him to be a man who could easily be thought of as handsome, but he has a rapist's eyes." Now, what on earth are a rapist's eyes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: So what we're talking about here is a proposal for a book that was never used, that was never written --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, please, Mr. Sweeney? We don't have all day, I'm afraid. We have to concentrate on your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine. I'll answer. There was something cold and chilling about his eyes, and I found -- I can remember feeling discomfort about that point. I believe -- but what I'm being asked about here is a proposal for a book which was never written, so that I'm -- and I feel -- asked about it now, I feel uncomfortable about the phrase. How do I know what's going inside that man's head? So, for example -- well, it's certainly no part whatsoever of the documentary. Put to me now, I regret the phrase. I don't know. It's not a good phrase. I shouldn't have used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you just denied any sensationalism and that kind of leans that way, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I said I wouldn't have used that word. It's not a word I like using. I don't like using the word "comfortable" either. But being reminded of it, "a rapist's eyes" strikes me as being a bad phrase, because it means -- it implies I've got some knowledge of what's inside this man's mind, and I don't. And no good reporter should ever say, "Ooh, he was thinking this," because how do I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just one more little area to go into and then I'll be finished, and to do that I think we need to go into private session, for reasons that we went into private session earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And these relate to the security of individuals?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall go into private session, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In any event, we all appreciate that Edward R. Murrow was known for his fairness and objectivity; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of trying to go down the middle, for being fair to both sides if he could.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, fairness and objective, but he was also willing to strike what he thought was cant. You can't watch -- being given some of his old documentaries to watch, and when he struck out against Senator McCarthy, that was brave and passionate reporting and he was taking a position there as well, on evidence, but he was taking a stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I totally agree with that. Just as you've taken a stand on little Krusa. That has been something that you're an expert on and something you've written about, something you're deeply passionate about. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I would -- I wouldn't want to say that. Well, it certainly feels to me, for example, by some of the other things I've been asked about, I'm much less of an expert. I did my best to report what happened in little Krusa as fairly and accurately as I could do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you condemned what happened in little Krusa?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, a hundred -- as I believe our films -- my reporting to be correct, a hundred people were killed in cold blood, men and boys. Yes, I condemn that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Certainly, sir. We all do. And I want to ask you about the KLA. You said you were skeptical about the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And you also recognise the power of propaganda, as you put it, of the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it you also recognise, since you're an experienced reporter in Kosovo, that the KLA used ruthless and brutal tactics on many occasions against both Serb security forces and Serbian civilians.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know of situations, for example, where the KLA kidnapped and shot Serb security forces and sometimes just ordinary Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I believe that happened, yes. And I've reported on it a couple of times, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then the KLA would sometimes just leave the police to pick up the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: The nature of -- yes, that would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And specifically - and I'll do just one example - in little Hoxha, about 10 miles from little Krusa, two Serb brothers were kidnapped and mutilated by KLA forces.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know the precise date. Maybe you can enlighten us.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I can't remember -- I don't know when -- I think that happened after NATO invaded, entered the country. That's my memory of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And, given the brutality of the Kosovo Liberation Army forces, I take it that, if you had a chance to do it, you would have done a documentary about those atrocities, too. Isn't that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: No, because the numbers don't match. We're talking about two dead in that particular example and a hundred dead in little Krusa. So there is no parity in the number of people who were murdered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So whether you do a documentary, then, depends upon numbers and not to show a pattern of brutality. Is that correct? You only want to show numbers; you don't want to show a pattern of brutal conduct, as you well could have, with the Kosovo Liberation Army? You can answer that yes or no, and I ask you to do that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Can you formulate the question so I can say yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. What appears to be important to you is numbers, so that even though, as you've testified, there's a pattern of conduct by the Kosovo Liberation Army showing ruthless and brutal tactics against both Serb security forces and Serb civilians, including kidnapping and murder, just because it was a smaller number, for example, than a hundred, you wouldn't be interested in doing a documentary concerning that conduct. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: May I answer in this way: That if I'd seen evidence of 800.000 Serbs fleeing the mountainside and them saying that they had been victims of many, many massacres, then I would have done a documentary on that because that's the evidence. Here, there was no doubt in my mind so many people, hundreds of thousands of people, fled what they said was Serb persecution. The massacre numbers --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You interviewed hundreds of thousands of people, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: No, of course I didn't, but I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Hold on a second. But I was on a hill-side, where you would wake up in the morning, or whatever, and then you'd see thousands of people walk by you during the day; you would see the television news, other reporters who you trust telling you the same story; and then the next morning, the same. Endless track -- I do not think it was a fiction. But I take the -- I'll answer the point. If I saw a parity of violence, I would have reported that. But what was so striking was that it was unequal. Small numbers of Serbs dead; big numbers of Albanians dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And, of course, you're also aware of the fact that there were many, tens of thousands of Serbs who left during the NATO bombing. You're aware of that, sir, are you not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Indeed, I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of General Lazarevic has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you believe, Mr. Sweeney, that it is a little bit speculative to say that, if you had seen 700.000 Serbs fleeing from Kosovo, you would have done a documentary. If there had never been 700.000 Serbs -- there were only 10 per cent of Serbs in the population, because as the numbers stand, if 700.000 Serbs had been there, then it would have taken 7 million Albanians to flee. If you look at the numbers proportionately, how many -- in proportion, how many Serbs fled from the NATO air-strikes and how many Albanians fled? That's one question. Second, you said a moment ago that you had been following the situation in Yugoslavia. Did you maybe film a documentary about the Serbs fleeing from Operation Storm and Flash, or were you filming only things that were convenient to Britain and the NATO alliance? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Thank you. The first question: I believe that I accurately and fairly reported what I saw on the ground, which is a huge number, hundreds of thousands of Albanians fleeing what they said was Serb persecution and killing. Second question: I started in 1991, and one of the things I reported was the murder of Serb civilians by Croat death squads, led by a Hungarian Croat fascist called Eduard Flores. Now, a friend of mine called Paul Janks investigated this story of how this group of lunatics in Osijek went around killing people, most of whom were innocent Serbs. And I did a documentary about it. Paul Janks himself was killed, I believe, by one of the Croat fascists. So I'm wholly familiar with what happened in Croatia: Violence upon violence; different communities killing each other. And I'm wholly aware, in my view, that all of the communities were guilty of barbarism from time to time. But, as I said, what happened -- what I saw in Kosovo and in little Krusa in 1999 was what I was told was Serb oppression, and as far as I can tell, as fairly and accurately as I told the story, that more than a hundred men and boys, Albanian men and boys, were murdered by their Serb neighbours and the Serb police and the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I understood that part.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: But as to your --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My question was this: You noted yourself that later Albanians came and looted Serb houses, that's what you said; that Albanians took out of those houses what they needed before you came. And then Albanians came back after NATO came in and did what they did, what you called payback. But are there any Serbs left now in Mala Krusa, where Serbs and Albanians lived half/half? Why didn't you film a documentary on that if you are involved in objective journalism? I personally think you are not. That's the point, if you agree with me.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: My answer to your question is that, after the massacre, the Albanians would not live with the Serbs and that's why they burned down their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I had sat down.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Okay. Nema problema. The answer to the question is that, after the massacre, the Albanians wouldn't want to live with the Serbs. Today there are no Serbs living in that village. That's a great tragedy. But at the same time, the people who precipitated that tragedy, who made it happen, were the people who carried out the massacre. So that the Albanians burned down the houses was wrong and stupid; it was foolish. They were biting off -- whatever they did was wrong. But as a moral wrong, it's nowhere near as bad as killing a hundred of your neighbours. And I believe that is what happened in that village. Now, you said earlier -- sorry, just to finish a point. You said there's a problem of "you doing NATO propaganda." Your colleague sort of did raise the story I did about how NATO had been lying when it said it hit the Chinese embassy in Belgrade by mistake. So I would say that there aren't that many British journalists who are willing to say -- for example, to take the line of the Chinese government against the line of the British government on a story as big and as important as that, which means that when I say that I believe this was a massacre -- now -- carried out by the Serbs against the Albanians, I believe that to be the case. Remember that I'm very skeptical of people in KLA uniform, but most of the stories I got was from the mothers and the daughters of the dead men and the six survivors that we managed to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I don't hold it against you that you condemn the massacre in Krusa; I condemn it, too. It shouldn't have happened; we shouldn't be talking about this. There's no one in this room who wouldn't say that it wasn't wrong. But the point I was trying to make is that something else happened after the Albanians' departure. We were bombed in Belgrade and the building of the television was hit, and I didn't see you protest against that. And your colleague journalists were killed in their work-places. Your source in the NATO alliance was the lawyer of -- if your source had been the lawyer of the families, he would have told you that it was against Milosevic, but you didn't write about that. And your colleagues were hit by bombs very far away from Krusa, very far away from Krusa. Thank you. Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: To be fair to me, I believe I did criticise and condemn the bombing of the journalists and the TV station, as only journalists would. I don't believe that anybody should bomb journalists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic, do you have questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Will you be lengthy?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No. I have approximately maybe about 20 minutes' worth, so I should be able to complete most of it in the ten minutes we have left and then shortly after the break, if I'm counting the time correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sweeney. My name is Dan Ivetic and I would have some questions for you. Since our time is limited, I would ask you to pay close attention to my questions and try to give the most accurate and truthful and concise answer possible. Now, first of all, sir, when looking at the Mala Krusa tragedy, one of the matters that you testified about, and it's contained in your statement, is this list that you found of the local militia members that you said had been involved in this event, and I want to ask you a question about this. Am I correct that you went over this list with the persons that you interviewed and the individuals from the village, and they confirmed that all these people on this list were local Serbs from the Mala Krusa village? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I asked them, every single last one, but there were a key number of names who had been identified by the women, and it was those that we were at most pains to identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I believe you had said that you did not know what organisations they were a part of, but you did know for certain persons -- for instance, you did know that Dimitri Nikolic worked in a rakija factory before the war, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, he ran a cafe in town. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I didn't -- I didn't know that he ran a cafe in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: By the way, on the organisation point --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you the questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We've got time restraints we've got to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to tender in part, I think in similar fashion to what the Prosecution did previously with this exhibit from the bar table, Exhibit P2335, to the extent that some of the individuals that this witness has identified in his statement, there are names of -- there are these names on this list, and that would be page 2 of the exhibit, the response to ICTY request number 1098. And for the record, the following individuals appear on the list that the witness has provided and also appear on this exhibit as being individuals for whom the MUP has no information about. They are -- and these are the numbers from the exhibit: Number 6, Rasko Nikolic; number 7, Miladin Nikolic; number 8, Danilo Nikolic; number 11, Sveta Tasic; number 14, Golub Cvetkovic; number 15, Stanko Cvetkovic; number 16, Stanislav Stankovic; number 17, Pera Stankovic; number 18, Trajce Stankovic; number 21, Steva Petkovic; number 22, Golub Petkovic; number 26, Aleksandar Petkovic; and number 27, Darko Tasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller, any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We will admit that document to the extent that it deals with these various individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, to talk about certain other individuals for matters of witness security, I need to go into private session for about five questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask the interpreters if it's necessary to break at this stage? It may be. Yes, the information is it is, so we'll break for 20 minutes, since we had half an hour at the last break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sweeney, in your statement you describe your return -- your visit to Mala Krusa. Am I correct that this took place approximately two and a half months after the events that transpired when persons were said to be killed at the hay-barn and two and a half months after the witnesses you spoke with in Albania had left their home village?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I also correct that during the intervening two-and-a-half-month period, you have no objective personal knowledge of how the condition of the village might have changed during that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: No objective reporter could have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Am I also correct that when you first arrived in Mala Krusa, you immediately ran into a young lad named Fadil, 14 years old, who was from the village and was a relative of someone whom you -- or you believe was a relative of someone who had perished in the Batusha barn?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you met this young lad, he was carrying a Kalashnikov assault rifle and a knife, according to your statement at least. Do you recall if he was dressed in civilian clothes or a uniform at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: He has a makeshift uniform on, I think a military hat of some kind, a beret.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: His pistol was a toy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The Kalashnikov was real though?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the knife was real?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now do you know whether he -- whether there were other persons walking around with arms in Mala Krusa or the surrounding area at that point in time when you returned to the village on or about June, I think it, the 14th -- you said was probably the date you returned?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. It was not a huge number of KLA/UCK, but there was some around.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say these were KLA/UCK. Did all of them have on uniforms, or were some of them dressed in civilian a garb?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Not that many. We would have filmed them because there weren't that many people around at that time. So I can't remember seeing any KLA soldiers in uniform in little Krusa because I think we would have filmed them, because we were alert to the possibility of what were they up to now. There were certainly a small number of -- of men with guns around. That's all I can help you with I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough. Fair enough. Now, you go on to describe in your statement that you entered the homes of some of the local Serb villagers who were believed to be perpetrators of the killing, and you describe that these homes had been abandoned and "already been looted by the Albanians." Am I correct that by the time you arrived in Mala Krusa on about June 14th, 1999, almost all of the Serb households in that village had been looted by Albanians prior to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: I think that's too sweeping. The -- it was -- I could go into these homes and find clothes -- I think some of the clothes had been taken out of wardrobes and so forth but not all, and I certainly wouldn't be able to say that of every home. People -- so, for example, I'm thinking about some of the homes I went into. I was the first person to take some of the documents, some of the photographs, because they had remained undisturbed. But remember, I was looking for that kind of evidence rather than to sort of steal a bicycle or whatever might be -- might be left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Or valuables?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yeah. So I was looking for particular things.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, of the homes that were -- that had been looted by Albanians, were there a large number of homes that had been looted, at least in part, by Albanians prior to your arrival in Mala Krusa in June of --

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: They weren't -- well, the significant moment for us - and I was away on holiday when it happened - was when the Serb houses, which had been pretty much extant, were burnt and their roofs came off in the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about the time-period before you arrived.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm -- what we're talking about -- for example, I can remember there was -- in one house there was a cow which was -- had been cut with a scythe and it was dying but not yet dead, but the homes were -- were on the whole empty-ish. I -- yes. It seems as though there had been some evidence of some of -- obviously or presumably the Albanians going into these homes and looking for valuables.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, sir, that you have no way of confirming that in fact the same persons who looted the Serb homes are not the same persons that looted the other homes in the village, objectively speaking?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid I have to answer that in the context of everything else that I was aware of, and I would find it surprising -- in fact, very surprising --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: -- to draw that inference. Basically you're looking at the whole context, and you can see why the Albanians would have thought: Why can't I go and steal from my old Serb neighbours, given what had happened? But I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you there and did your film crew film any funeral or memorial service in Mala Krusa?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't there; the film crew was. I think I was on holiday. I had spent about a month on the trot there. Then I went away on home, and there was somebody else or another part of the team stayed on and filmed the funeral rites and there were lots of KLA soldiers there at the time. And I can remember James Miller talking about it and saying that -- you know, where had these buggers come from? We hadn't seen them before in -- in any numbers before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And these KLA soldiers that were present, they did a memorial gun salute to the persons -- victims that were buried?

utterances.speaker: JOHN SWEENEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's something I'd like to say, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. About what, Mr. Sweeney?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's actually about a matter which I believe ought to be heard in secret session about one of the other witnesses who were under some kind of protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into private session for that reason.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Ms. Moeller, I don't think I gave you an adequate opportunity to deal with the exhibits, now that I look at the state of the numbering. There must be numbers to be attached to certain exhibits. So could you please do the exercise of identifying what we should be considering in the way of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, most certainly, Your Honours. The first documentary Witness to Murder is Exhibit P114; the second documentary Prime Suspects is Exhibit Number P115; then the clip from the raw footage that we also seek to tender is Exhibit P2364. In the meantime, we have also provided an exhibit P number for the sequence of the ten video-clips that were shown in court today, and we could make available a CD-ROM with these clips to the Bench, and this would be Exhibit Number P2384 just so that it is clear on the transcript then to which specific clips the testimony related. And in addition to these exhibits, I would also seek to tender Exhibit Number P2328 and 2327, which are the notebook and the list of names that appear in the documentary and that were addressed today with the witness in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you have some re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, these various exhibits are admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's always possible for witnesses who come here, Mr. Sweeney, to leave with the impression that they've been rushed. Inevitably, we're covering a very large area and very large number of events; this is a significant one, and therefore your contribution is important. But you have to bear in mind also that we've heard from some eye-witnesses directly ourselves. There is other material relating to these events, so we have to put your evidence into context. We're extremely grateful to you for coming to give that evidence, and you're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we break for the day, I would also wish to tender from the bar some exhumation reports in relation to the site Krusha e Vogel because we completed leading evidence on this site at this point, and I think the fact that bones were fact near the Drin River was referred to by several witnesses and we have corresponding exhumation material that I would seek to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what are the reports that you seek to tender, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: These are reports from the Metropolitan Police, the anti-terrorist branch from the United Kingdom, and it's a series of individual reports of exhumation activities undertaken in Krusha e Vogel at different locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What are the numbers of these?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The numbers are Exhibit P100, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106, 107, 110, 111, and 112. These are reports and photos, and I cannot really tell Your Honours why they all have separate P numbers, but they all pertain to the same site and the same exhumation operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do any of these identify any victims?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: They identify -- no, they do not identify any of the victims from the barn. They only speak about bone fragments having been found and some other material, shoes, et cetera, at different locations along and in the close vicinity of the Drin River. But they do not -- there is no identification of these men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Your Honour, without -- and I thought that the persons -- the forensic persons were going to testify with respect to these documents; without that, I don't know what probative value they have. Secondly, I do not know -- these particular exhibits were not referenced with respect to this witness, so I did not take the time to go through them one by one. I'd like to know from the other side whether these are all of the Mala Krusa exhumation reports, since when I did review them previously, as I recall there were a fair number of them that dealt with bones and bone fragments that turned out not to be human bones. So I don't know whether this is the -- whether these exhibit numbers that have been listed are the entire set of forensic documents, which include verification that some of the remains found were non-human, or if this is just a selective view of them. If they are going to come in - and I would still think that there should be an objection to that - but if the Court were to overrule that objection, I think that it's either all or nothing should come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what we'll do is give you an opportunity to review this material, and we'll postpone a decision on it until sometime next week. We'll give you time to discuss it with the Prosecution, and I leave it to you to alert us again sometime before -- before Thursday -- on or before Thursday of next week of your respective positions in relation to this, and we'll make a decision at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: -- just respond to one inquiry directly. These are all the reports that are on our exhibit list in relation to Krusha e Vogel. So it's a complete set of what we intended to tender from the start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Well, that brings us to the end of this week, and we'll resume at 9.00 on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 16th day of October, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 16 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
